entities.name: password spraying
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors deploy password spraying techniques, using tools such as SharpDomainSpray to gain access to account credentials [T1110.003].

entities.name: exploiting router’s IP address
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors gained initial access through the Secure Shell (SSH) protocol by exploiting a router’s IP address [T1021.004].

entities.name: exploiting Veeam Backup and Replication component
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors exploit publicly available vulnerabilities, such as those found in the Veeam Backup and Replication component of unpatched Veeam backup servers [T1068] (CVE-2023-27532 and CVE-2024-40711).

entities.name: using VB scripts
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors frequently execute malicious commands by using Visual Basic (VB) scripts [T1059.005].

entities.name: creating domain accounts
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors attempt to establish persistence by creating new domain accounts [T1136.002] to abuse the functions of domain controllers.

entities.name: Kerberoasting
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors leverage post-exploitation techniques, such as Kerberoasting, to extract credentials stored in the process memory of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS) [T1003.001].

entities.name: credential scraping
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors use credential scraping tools [T1003], like Mimikatz and LaZagne, to aid in privilege escalation.

entities.name: network discovery and reconnaissance
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors use tools like SoftPerfect, Advanced IP Scanner, and NetScan [T1016] for network discovery and reconnaissance.

entities.name: using nltest /dclist: and nltest /DOMAIN_TRUSTS
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors use nltest /dclist: and nltest /DOMAIN_TRUSTS [T1018][T1482] for network and domain discovery.

entities.name: disabling security software
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors disable security software to avoid detection. Cybersecurity researchers observed Akira threat actors using PowerTool to exploit the Zemana AntiMalware driver and terminate antivirus-related processes [T1562.001].

entities.name: abusing remote access tools
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors abuse remote access tools such as AnyDesk and LogMeIn [T1219] to maintain persistence and blend in with administrator activity.

entities.name: using Impacket
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors leverage Impacket (an open source tool designed for network protocol manipulation) to execute the remote command wmiexec.py.

entities.name: uninstalling EDR systems
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors implement techniques such as uninstalling endpoint detection and response (EDR) systems [T1562.001].

entities.name: creating new user accounts
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors create new user accounts and add them to the administrator group to establish a foothold in the environment [T1136.001].

entities.name: bypassing VMDK file protection
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors bypassed Virtual Machine Disk (VMDK) file protection by temporarily powering down the domain controller’s VM, copying the VMDK files, and attaching them to a newly created VM.

entities.name: leveraging Veeam.Backup.MountService.exe
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors have also been observed leveraging services like Veeam.Backup.MountService.exe for privilege escalation (CVE-2024-40711) [T1068].

entities.name: using legitimate remote access tools
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors use legitimate remote access tools like AnyDesk or LogMeIn [T1219] to pivot laterally.

entities.name: using RDP
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors also employ RDP [T1021.001], SSH [T1021.004], and MobaXterm to expand their presence within the compromised network [T1021].

entities.name: using tunneling utilities
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors establish command and control (C2) communications by using tunneling utilities, such as Ngrok [T1572], to initiate encrypted sessions that bypass perimeter monitoring.

entities.name: using PowerShell and WMIC
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors use PowerShell and Windows Management Instrumentation Command-line (WMIC) [T1059.001] to disable services and execute malicious scripts.

entities.name: data collection
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors leverage tools such as FileZilla and WinRAR to collect data [T1560.001].

entities.name: data exfiltration
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors use WinSCP and RClone to exfiltrate data [T1048].

entities.name: using AnyDesk, MobaXterm, RustDesk, and Cloudflare Tunnel
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors leverage readily available tools like AnyDesk, MobaXterm, RustDesk, and Cloudflare Tunnel to exfiltrate data through various protocols such as FTP, SFTP, and cloud storage services like Mega [T1537].

entities.name: using Ngrok for data exfiltration
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors use Ngrok to create secure tunnels for data exfiltration [T1090].

entities.name: double-extortion model
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors use a double-extortion model [T1657], which involves threat actors both encrypting systems [T1486] and threatening to leak sensitive information.

entities.name: using .onion URLs
entities.evidence: The Akira ransom note provides each company with a unique code and instructions to contact the threat actors via a .onion URL, which is accessible through the Tor network [T1090.003][T1573.002].

entities.name: using Bitcoin for ransom payments
entities.evidence: Victims make ransom payments by using Bitcoin to cryptocurrency-wallet addresses provided by the Akira threat actors.

entities.name: threatening to publish exfiltrated data
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors threaten to publish exfiltrated data on the Tor network, and in some instances have called victimized companies, according to FBI reporting.

entities.name: using ChaCha20 stream cipher and RSA public-key cryptosystem
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors use a sophisticated hybrid encryption scheme to lock data. This involves combining a ChaCha20 stream cipher with an RSA public-key cryptosystem for a fast and secure key exchange [T1486].

entities.name: using .akira or .powerranges extensions
entities.evidence: Encrypted files are appended with a .akira or .powerranges extension.

entities.name: using .akiranew or .aki extensions
entities.evidence: With the new Akira_v2 variant, encrypted files are appended either with an .akira or .powerranges extension, or with .akiranew or .aki.

entities.name: Create Account: Domain Account
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors attempt to abuse the functions of domain controllers by creating new domain accounts to establish persistence.

entities.name: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors exploit unpatched software vulnerabilities (e.g., Veeam Backup and Replication CVEs) to gain elevated privileges on hosts or servers (enabling access to sensitive data), and for credential harvesting.

entities.name: Obfuscated Files or Information

entities.name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Compression

entities.name: Masquerading
entities.evidence: Akira threat actors disguise malicious files and payloads to appear legitimate.

entities.name: File and Directory Permissions Modification: Windows File and Directory Permissions Modification

entities.name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools

entities.name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify System Firewall

entities.name: Proxy Through Victim

entities.name: OS Credential Dumping: NTDS

entities.name: Brute Force

entities.name: Brute Force: Password Spraying

entities.name: Credentials from Password Stores: Windows Credential Manager

relationships.target: exploiting Veeam Backup and Replication component
relationships.evidence: Akira threat actors exploit publicly available vulnerabilities, such as those found in the Vee, Veeam Backup and Replication component of unpatched Veeam backup servers [T1068] (CVE-2023-27532 and CVE-2024-40711).
Akira threat actors frequently execute malicious commands by using Visual Basic (VB) scripts [T1059.005].
Akira threat actors attempt to establish persistence by creating new domain accounts [T1136.002] to abuse the functions of domain controllers.
Akira threat actors use credential scraping tools [T1003], like Mimikatz and LaZagne, to aid in privilege escalation.
Akira threat actors use tools like SoftPerfect, Advanced IP Scanner, and NetScan [T1016] for network discovery and reconnaissance.
Akira threat actors use nltest /dclist: and nltest /DOMAIN_TRUSTS [T1018][T1482] for network and domain discovery.

Akira threat actors disable security software to avoid detection. Cybersecurity researchers observed Akira threat actors using PowerTool to exploit the Zemana AntiMalware driver and terminate antivirus-related processes [T1562.001].
Akira threat actors abuse remote access tools such as AnyDesk and LogMeIn [T1219] to maintain persistence and blend in with administrator activity.
Akira threat actors leverage Impacket (an open source tool designed for network protocol manipulation) to execute the remote command wmiexec.py.
Akira threat actors implement techniques such as uninstalling endpoint detection and response (EDR) systems [T1562.001].
Akira threat actors create new user accounts and add them to the administrator group to establish a foothold in the environment [T1136.001].
Akira threat actors bypassed Virtual Machine Disk (VMDK) file protection by temporarily powering down the domain controller’s VM, copying the VMDK files, and attaching them to a newly created VM.
Akira threat actors have also been observed leveraging services like Veeam.Backup.MountService.exe for privilege escalation (CVE-2024-40711) [T1068].
Akira threat actors use legitimate remote access tools like AnyDesk or LogMeIn [T1219] to pivot laterally.
Akira threat actors also employ RDP [T1021.001], SSH [T1021.004], and MobaXterm to expand their presence within the compromised network [T1021].
Akira threat actors establish command and control (C2) communications by using tunneling utilities, such as Ngrok [T1572], to initiate encrypted sessions that bypass perimeter monitoring.
Akira threat actors use PowerShell and Windows Management Instrumentation Command-line (WMIC) [T1059.001] to disable services and execute malicious scripts.
Akira threat actors leverage tools such as FileZilla and WinRAR to collect data [T1560.001].
Akira threat actors use WinSCP and RClone to exfiltrate data [T1048].

relationships.target: using AnyDesk, MobaXterm, RustDesk, and Cloudflare Tunnel
relationships.evidence: Akira threat actors leverage readily available tools like AnyDesk, MobaXterm, RustDesk, and Cloudflare Tunnel to exfiltrate data through various protocols such as FTP, SFTP, and cloud storage services like Mega [T1537].
Akira threat actors use Ngrok to create secure tunnels for data exfiltration [T1090].
Akira threat actors use a double-extortion model [T1657], which involves threat actors both encrypting systems [T1486] and threatening to leak sensitive information.
The Akira ransom note provides each company with a unique code and instructions to contact the threat actors via a .onion URL, which is accessible through the Tor network [T1090.003][T1573.002].
Victims make ransom payments by using Bitcoin to cryptocurrency-wallet addresses provided by the Akira threat actors.
Akira threat actors threaten to publish exfiltrated data on the Tor network, and in some instances have called victimized companies, according to FBI reporting.

relationships.target: using ChaCha20 stream cipher and RSA public-key cryptosystem
relationships.evidence: Akira threat actors use a sophisticated hybrid encryption scheme to lock data. This involves combining a ChaCha20 stream cipher with an RSA public-key cryptosystem for a fast and secure key exchange [T1486].
Encrypted files are appended with a .akira or .powerranges extension.
With the new Akira_v2 variant, encrypted files are appended either with an .akira or .powerranges extension, or with .akiranew or .aki.

Akira threat actors use a sophisticated hybrid encryption scheme to lock data. This involves combining a ChaCha20 stream cipher with an RSA public-key cryptosystem for a fast and secure key exchange [T1486].
Akira’s encryptor (w.exe) uses PowerShell commands to delete Volume Shadow Copy Service (VSS) copies on Windows systems [T1490].
With the new Akira_v2 variant, encrypted files are appended either with an .akira or .powerranges extension, or with .akiranew or .aki.
Additionally, a ransom note named fn.txt or akira_readme.txt appears in both the root directory (C:) and each user’s home directory (C:\Users).

A free, open source FTP (including SSH FTP), WebDAV, Amazon S3, and secure copy protocol client. Akira threat actors use it to transfer data from a compromised network to actor-controlled accounts.
